title: What's the plan? Metrics for implicit planning in LLMs and their application to rhyme generation and question answering
claim: Across model families and sizes, unsteered regeneration of the original outcome class exceeds chance, and the effect grows with scale and instruction tuning.
layout: 1 panel, grouped bar chart, left-to-right, dashed family separators, hatched baseline bars
description: A single wide grouped bar chart titled 'Rhyme Family Regeneration: Correct vs Baseline'. The x-axis lists about 24 models: Gemma2, Gemma3, Llama3 and Qwen3, each in instruction-tuned and Base variants. The y-axis is Regeneration Rate, from 0 to 0.25. Each model has a solid colored bar for correct regeneration (same rhyme family) beside a hatched, lighter bar for the baseline (average of other rhyme families). Colors separate families: blue, orange, green and red. Dashed vertical lines divide the groups. A legend in the top right explains solid versus hatched. The solid bars are far above the flat baseline of about 0.02, mostly for larger instruction-tuned models. The tallest bar is Gemma3_27B at about 0.25. Base models and small models show smaller margins. The eye goes first to the tall orange bars on the left.
caption: Comparison of unsteered regeneration rates to baseline chance level for the model. \revised{During regeneration with stochastic sampling, some rhyme families are expected to occur with non-zero frequency by chance. We estimate the baseline chance level that unsteered regeneration rate must exceed to show evidence for successful backward planning as the average frequency of rhyme families other than the one in whose context the couplet's second line was originally generated by the model.}
abstract: Prior work suggests that language models, while trained on next token prediction, show implicit planning behavior: they may select the next token in preparation to a predicted future token, such as a likely rhyming word, as supported by a prior qualitative study of Claude 3.5 Haiku using a cross-layer transcoder. We propose much simpler techniques for assessing implicit planning in language models. With case studies on rhyme poetry generation and question answering, we demonstrate that our methodology easily scales to many models. Across models, we find that the generated rhyme (e.g. "-ight") or answer to a question ("whale") can be manipulated by steering at the end of the preceding line with a vector, affecting the generation of intermediate tokens leading up to the rhyme or answer word. We show that implicit planning is a universal mechanism, present in smaller models than previously thought, starting from 1B parameters. Our methodology offers a widely applicable direct way to study implicit planning abilities of LLMs. More broadly, understanding planning abilities of language models can inform decisions in AI safety and control.
